sections.section_heading: How does it work in the first ten minutes?
sections.description:
One input, and the rest runs unattended. Every step except your two minutes targets under ten minutes.

We do not ask you what industry you are in. Your website already says. Ladder7 reads it the way a good consultant would, reaches a conclusion, and reaches it again from scratch whenever your site changes or you ask it to look again.

There is no dropdown, because asking an owner whether they are "professional services" or "trades" is asking them to translate their business into our vocabulary, and a wrong answer would then carry the highest trust in the system. If you never answer the seven questions, the system proceeds and flags the gaps rather than hanging.

sections.section_heading: Ten executives, each with a written mandate
sections.description:
Most AI products give you one assistant. This gives you a company. Each executive has an explicit scope, defined hand-offs and a deliverable specification.

Behind those ten sit fifty specialists across eleven divisions: a cash forecaster, a lead qualifier, a pipeline keeper, a churn analyst and the rest. An executive can ask its own specialists for depth, and the answer comes back to the executive, who stays responsible for it.

Four rules keep that from becoming a free-for-all. An executive can only ask its own team, resolved from the org chart at call time rather than from the model's request. Delegation is capped at two levels. A delegated run shares the caller's budget, so an executive that delegates five times has spent its own allowance rather than five more. And delegation can never raise permissions.

sections.section_heading: It tells you what it could not determine
sections.description:
An agent that never says "I could not find this" is an agent filling gaps, and you would have no way of telling which sentences those were.

Every brief ends with a mandatory section: what the executive could not determine, the gap that would most improve the next report, and the cheapest way to close it. Every mandate also carries one rule, which is never to present a number it cannot source.

sections.description:
Every action is classified by blast radius, and permission attaches to the action rather than to the agent.

Content crawled from a third-party site is marked untrusted, is never placed into a system prompt, and any action in a run that touched it is escalated to T2 at minimum regardless of its normal tier. There is also a monthly spend cap per account, enforced before any model call. Executives earn the right to act unsupervised on low-risk work by building a track record you can see, with a mandatory 10 percent audit sample so the signal never dies, and never on the risky kind.

content.text: A LITTLE MORE CLARITY
Good questions.
What is L7 Nexus?–
A leased AI executive team. It builds a permanent company brain from your website, runs ten named executives and fifty specialists against it, and returns one decision per board review.
Will it make things up?+

Every mandate forbids presenting a number it cannot source, and every brief ends with what it could not determine and the cheapest way to close that gap. You can see which questions stayed open rather than guessing which sentences were invented.
Do I own my data, or am I locked in?+
You own it. The brain is markdown in a folder you can download right now and open in Obsidian. Leaving costs you nothing but the executives.
Can it email my customers or change my accounting records?+

No. The only email that ships goes to the account owner, and its recipient is resolved on the server, so there is no address field an injected web page could reach. No integration writes to your books or your CRM today.
How much does a board review cost to run?+
Roughly $10 to $25 for a full review, meaning ten agent loops plus their specialist benches. Today every account runs them free.
Who is L7 Nexus not for?+
